skills.title: Data structures
skills.summary: Arrays, linked lists, stacks, queues, hash maps and trees, and when each fits

concepts.title: Hash map
concepts.summary: Key-value lookup in constant time on average, by hashing the key to a bucket

variants.q: You look up a key in a hash map holding `n` entries. What is the typical (average-case) cost?
variants.explain: The key's hash points straight at a bucket, so on average only a few entries are checked whatever the size. O(log n) is a balanced tree, such as a sorted map.

variants.q: A hash map's lookups slow down badly even though it holds only a few thousand entries. What is the most likely cause?
choices: Many keys hash to the same bucket, so lookups scan long chains
The keys are strings, which hash slower than integers
The map wasn't re-sorted after the last batch of inserts
Hash maps get slower once they pass 1,000 entries
variants.explain: With a poor hash function (or keys chosen to collide), entries pile into a few buckets and lookups degrade toward O(n). That's why many runtimes use randomised or seeded hashes.

concepts.title: Stack vs queue
concepts.summary: Last-in-first-out vs first-in-first-out, and which problems need which

variants.q: Breadth-first search visits a graph level by level, nearest nodes first. Which structure holds the nodes waiting to be visited?
choices: A min-heap keyed by node id
variants.explain: A FIFO queue hands back nodes in the order they were found, which is level by level. Swapping in a stack (LIFO) turns it into depth-first search.

variants.q: You check whether brackets like `{[()]}` are balanced by reading left to right. Which structure fits?
choices: A sorted list of bracket positions
variants.explain: The most recent unclosed opener must be the first one closed, which is LIFO. Counters alone accept `([)]`, which isn't balanced.

concepts.title: Array vs linked list
concepts.summary: Contiguous storage with fast indexing vs linked nodes with cheap inserts at a known spot

variants.q: You need to insert at the front of a sequence of `n` items. What does it cost in an array vs a singly linked list?
variants.explain: An array has to shift every element one slot to make room. A linked list just points a new node at the old head.

variants.q: You need the element at position `i` of a sequence of `n` items. What does it cost in an array vs a singly linked list?
choices: Array O(log n), linked list O(n)
variants.explain: An array computes the address of slot `i` directly. A linked list has to follow `i` pointers from the head.

concepts.title: Cache locality
concepts.summary: Data laid out next to each other in memory is much faster to walk, even at the same Big O

variants.q: Summing 10 million integers takes O(n) whether they're in an array or a linked list, yet the array is several times faster. Why?
choices: Arrays are always allocated on the stack, where access is faster
Neighbouring values share a cache line, so reads mostly hit the cache
Linked lists check bounds on every step they take
The compiler turns the array loop into an O(log n) one
variants.explain: Walking contiguous memory uses every byte of each cache line and lets the prefetcher run ahead. A linked list's nodes are scattered, so many steps wait on a cache miss.

choices: The compiler can only vectorise the outer loop
Go checks bounds less often in the swapped order
Each row is contiguous, so a row is read in memory order
The swapped loop does fewer total iterations
variants.explain: Each `grid[r]` is its own contiguous slice. Going down a column jumps to a different row on every step and misses the cache; going along a row reads neighbouring values.

variants.q: A program sums the `id` field of 10 million records, each a 200-byte struct. Keeping the ids in their own array makes the sum several times faster, though both versions are O(n). Why?
choices: The CPU skips the comparisons for the other fields
The smaller array is compiled into an O(log n) loop
The ids can be kept in registers instead of memory
Each cache line then holds many ids instead of one id plus unused bytes
variants.explain: The work is the same, but a cache line fetched from memory is now full of useful ids rather than mostly bytes of other fields. Big O ignores this constant factor, which is where the speed-up comes from.

concepts.title: Binary heap (priority queue)
concepts.summary: A tree kept in an array that always gives the smallest (or largest) item cheaply

variants.q: You read a stream of events too large to keep in memory and must report the 10 with the highest scores. What's the best structure?
choices: A list of every event, sorted at the end
A max-heap holding the 10 best seen so far
A hash set of the scores seen so far
A min-heap holding the 10 best seen so far
variants.explain: Keep 10 items; when a new one beats the heap's minimum (its root), replace it. That's O(n log k) time and O(k) memory. A max-heap puts the best item at the root, so finding the one to evict means scanning all 10.

variants.q: A binary min-heap holds `n` items. What do peeking at the minimum and removing it cost?
choices: Peek O(log n), remove O(log n)
variants.explain: The minimum always sits at the root, so peeking is O(1). Removing it moves the last item to the root and sifts it down one level at a time, which is O(log n).

concepts.title: Ring buffer
concepts.summary: A fixed-size array that wraps around, overwriting the oldest item when full

variants.q: A service must always keep its last 1,000 log lines in memory for a debug endpoint, using a fixed amount of memory. What fits best?
choices: A list that you trim to 1,000 every hour
A hash map keyed by timestamp
variants.explain: A ring buffer writes each new line over the oldest one in O(1), so memory never grows. A list trimmed occasionally grows without bound between trims.

variants.q: A ring buffer has 5 slots. You write the values 1 to 7 in order. Which values does it hold now?
variants.explain: Writes 6 and 7 wrap around and overwrite the two oldest values, 1 and 2. A ring buffer always holds the most recent writes.

concepts.title: Bloom filter
concepts.summary: A compact set that can say "definitely not present" or "maybe present"

variants.q: A Bloom filter of seen URLs says a URL is **not** in the set. What do you know?
choices: It is probably not in the set
It might still be in the set if the filter is full
Nothing until you check the source of truth
It is definitely not in the set
variants.explain: Bloom filters have no false negatives: an added item always sets all its bits. They do have false positives, so a "maybe" answer still needs checking.

variants.q: Before querying the database, a sign-up form checks a Bloom filter of taken usernames. The filter says "present". What should the code do?
choices: Query the database, since it may be a false positive
Reject the name: the filter is never wrong
Add the name to the filter again
Accept the name: "present" is usually wrong
variants.explain: "Present" means "maybe": the bits could have been set by other names. The filter saves database hits only for the "definitely not" answers.

skills.title: Big O
skills.summary: Reading the time and space cost of code and picking an algorithm for the data size

concepts.title: Quadratic time, O(n²)
concepts.summary: Work that grows with the square of the input, typically from comparing every pair

variants.explain: The inner loop runs n−1, n−2, … 1 times, about n²/2 comparisons in all. Halving the work only changes a constant, so it's still O(n²); a hash set makes it O(n).

variants.q: A job compares every user with every other user to find possible duplicates. Users grow from 10,000 to 20,000. Roughly how much longer does the job take?
variants.explain: Comparing all pairs is O(n²), so doubling n multiplies the work by about four.
Starting `j` at `i + 1` visits each pair once: n(n-1)/2, about 500,000 for n = 1,000. It's still O(n²); the 1,000,000 figure would be a loop that compares every item with every item.
Nested loops multiply: 100 × 100 × 100. Adding the sizes (300) is what sequential, not nested, loops would cost.

concepts.title: Hidden O(n) inside a loop
concepts.summary: A built-in like `includes` or `in list` that scans on every call turns a loop quadratic

variants.q:
`users` has n items and `activeIds` (an array) has m. What is the time complexity, and what's the usual fix?

```ts
const active = users.filter((u) => activeIds.includes(u.id))
```
variants.explain: `includes` scans the array on every call, so the filter does up to n·m comparisons. A `Set` lookup is O(1) on average, making it O(n + m).
`slices.Contains` is a linear scan, run once per order. Building a `map[string]struct{}` from `blocked` first makes each check O(1) on average.

variants.q:
`users` has n items and `active_ids` (a `list`) has m. What is the time complexity, and what's the usual fix?

```python
active = [u for u in users if u.id in active_ids]
```
choices: O(n); `in` on a list is a constant-time check
O(n log m); `in` uses binary search
O(n + m); Python caches the lookups
variants.explain: `in` on a list scans it element by element, once per user. On a `set` it's a hash lookup, O(1) on average.

variants.q:
`items` has n entries. What is the time complexity of this deduplication, and what's the usual fix?

```text
result = []
for x in items:
    if not result.contains(x):
        result.append(x)
```
choices: O(n); `contains` on a list is a constant-time check
O(n²) in the worst case; track seen items in a hash set
O(n log n); `contains` binary-searches the list
O(n); appending to the list is the slow part
variants.explain: `contains` on a list scans it, and the list grows to n entries, so n calls cost O(n²) overall. A hash set makes each check O(1) on average.

concepts.title: Logarithmic time, O(log n)
concepts.summary: Work that grows by one step each time the input doubles, as in binary search

variants.q: Binary search on a sorted list of 1,000,000 items. About how many comparisons does it need at most?
variants.explain: Each comparison halves what's left, and 2²⁰ is just over a million. That's what O(log n) means in practice.

variants.q: An O(log n) lookup takes 30 steps on a table. The table grows to twice its size. How many steps now, roughly?
variants.explain: Doubling the input adds one more halving step to a log₂ algorithm. That's why logarithmic structures scale so well.

concepts.title: Amortized O(1)
concepts.summary: An operation that's occasionally expensive but cheap on average over many calls, like appending to a dynamic array

variants.q: Go's `append` sometimes copies the whole slice into a bigger array. Why is appending still considered O(1)?
choices: The copy runs in a background goroutine
Capacity grows by a multiple, so n appends copy O(n) items in total
The garbage collector does the copy, so it isn't counted
`append` copies only when the slice is shared with another
variants.explain: Growing by a multiple (not a fixed amount) means the copies add up to O(n) over n appends, so each append is O(1) on average. Preallocating with `make([]T, 0, n)` skips the copies.

variants.q: Most `push` calls on a JavaScript array are fast, but now and then one is slow while the engine moves the array to a bigger buffer. What's the cost of `push` over many calls?
choices: O(n) each, because of the occasional moves
O(1) amortized: the slow moves average out
Unbounded: it depends on garbage collection
variants.explain: Engines such as V8 grow the buffer by a multiple of its size, so the occasional O(n) move averages out to O(1) per push. Amortized describes the total over many calls, not every single call.

variants.q: In CPython, `list.append` occasionally has to reallocate and copy the list. What is the cost of `append` over many calls?
choices: O(n) each, because of the copies
O(1) only for lists under a size limit
variants.explain: CPython over-allocates by a fraction of the list's current size, so reallocations get rarer as it grows and average out to O(1) per append. Inserting at the front with `insert(0, x)` is O(n) every time.

variants.q: A dynamic array grows by a fixed 10 slots each time it's full, instead of doubling. Appending n items one at a time, what is the amortized cost per append?
variants.explain: Each growth copies everything so far, and growths happen only every 10 appends, so total copying is about n²/20 and the per-append average is O(n). Amortized O(1) needs capacity to grow by a multiple, like doubling.

concepts.title: Comparison sort lower bound
concepts.summary: No sort that only compares elements can beat O(n log n) in the worst case

variants.q: What is the best possible worst-case time for a sort that only compares pairs of elements?
variants.explain: There are n! possible orderings and each comparison can at best halve them, which takes about n log n comparisons. Merge sort and heapsort reach that bound.

variants.q: Counting sort sorts a million ages (0 to 120) in O(n + k). How does it get under O(n log n)?
choices: It runs its comparisons in parallel across cores
It counts each value's occurrences instead of comparing
O(n log n) only bounds the average case
It needs the input to be already nearly sorted
variants.explain: The lower bound applies only to comparison sorts. Counting and radix sorts exploit a small, known key range instead, so they don't compare elements.

concepts.title: Average vs worst case
concepts.summary: An algorithm can be fast on typical input and much slower on particular input

variants.q: A textbook quicksort always picks the first element as the pivot. What happens on input that's already sorted?
choices: It finishes in O(n), since nothing moves
It stays O(n log n), as on any input
variants.explain: Each pivot is the smallest item, so every partition splits off just one element and the recursion is n levels deep. Quicksort's O(n log n) is the average case, not a guarantee.

variants.q: Why do production quicksorts pick a random pivot or the median of three elements instead of the first one?
choices: To bring the average case down to O(n)
To make the sort stable for equal keys
To make it safe to run on several threads
To avoid O(n²) time on already-sorted input
variants.explain: With a first-element pivot, sorted input splits off one element per level; a random or median-of-three pivot keeps those partitions balanced. It doesn't make quicksort stable or linear, and the O(n²) worst case still exists for unlucky or crafted input.

concepts.title: Space complexity
concepts.summary: How much extra memory an algorithm needs as the input grows, call stack included

variants.explain: Each call waits on the next, so n stack frames are alive at the deepest point. A plain loop would be O(1), and a large enough array overflows the stack.
In the worst case (no duplicates) `seen` ends up holding all n values. That's the trade: O(n) time for O(n) extra space, versus a pairwise check using O(1) space and O(n²) time.
It swaps in place and only keeps two indexes. A version that allocates a second slice would use O(n).

variants.q: A balanced binary tree has n nodes. Which traversal needs more extra memory?
choices: Both need O(n), since each visits every node
Depth-first: the recursion keeps every node on the stack
Breadth-first: its queue can hold a whole level, about n/2 nodes
Neither: both run in O(1) extra space
variants.explain: Depth-first only holds the current path, O(log n) deep for a balanced tree, while breadth-first's queue holds a full level, O(n). Time is O(n) for both, but space is a separate question.

concepts.title: Big O drops constants
concepts.summary: Big O describes growth for large inputs; it ignores constant factors and small sizes

variants.q: Algorithm A's running time grows linearly with n, and algorithm B's grows quadratically. What does that guarantee?
choices: A is faster for every input size
B is faster for small inputs
Beyond some input size, A is faster
variants.explain: Big O only compares growth. A's constant factors can be large enough that B wins on small inputs, which is why many sort routines switch to insertion sort for short runs.

variants.q: An algorithm does `3n² + 50n + 1000` steps. What is its Big O?
variants.explain: Big O keeps only the fastest-growing term and drops its constant factor. For large n, `3n²` dwarfs the rest.
